request.system: You are clustering code review findings from one PR. Always respond with valid JSON.
request.prompt:
You are clustering code review findings from the same PR. For each PAIR below, decide whether the two findings describe the SAME underlying issue — same root cause in the same code location. Different wording is fine. A finding about a DIFFERENT defect in the same file or function is NOT the same issue. Severity or aspect differences of the same root cause ARE the same issue.


For THIS scoring pass, duplicate equivalence is stricter than sharing a root cause.
You must compare the COMPLETE MATERIAL CLAIMS, including mechanism, triggering
conditions, execution path, and consequence. The same line or broad concern does
not establish equivalence. A report of wrong-category selection, a case/rename
mismatch, a crash, and a silent fallback are different claims even at one lookup.
An inactive/unbound API concern and an alleged active user-facing failure differ.
A compound report with an additional material claim does NOT equal its subset.
Differences only in wording, severity, or hedging do not create separate claims.
If the claimed mechanisms, triggers or consequences conflict, or one report adds
an unsupported/different material factual claim, return same=false. You are NOT
verifying which claim is true; do not repair or reinterpret either report to make
them match. If unsure whether their full claims are equivalent, return false.

For every numbered pair, extract what A and B actually CLAIM into mechanism,
trigger and consequence. Then list material_differences and give your equivalence
verdict, confidence and reason. same=true requires no material differences.
Return ONLY this JSON object, with EVERY pair index exactly once:
{"pairs":[{"pair":1,"a":{"mechanism":"...","trigger":"...","consequence":"..."},"b":{"mechanism":"...","trigger":"...","consequence":"..."},"material_differences":[],"same":true,"confidence":0.9,"reason":"..."}]}

PAIRS:
PAIR 1:
A: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts:5 — The unbounded guests array permits arbitrarily large database writes, calendar payloads, translation work, and concurrent email fan-out per request.
B: Unbounded guests array (no max() on z.array in addGuests.schema.ts) with no rate limiting, combined with attendee authorization path — any authenticated attendee on any booking can create thousands of attendee rows and trigger thousands of invite emails in a single API call (email-bombing vector)

PAIR 2:
A: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts:5 — The unbounded guests array permits arbitrarily large database writes, calendar payloads, translation work, and concurrent email fan-out per request.
B: Unbounded guests array size on the input schema — no .max() on z.array(z.string().email()), allowing a single authenticated request to create arbitrary attendees and fan out emails and calendar writes (addGuests.schema.ts:5)

PAIR 3:
A: The write `prisma.booking.update({ where: { id: bookingId } })` re-derives authorization only from the earlier in-memory check with no ownership predicate in the update's where clause, and the guests are created before calendar/email work with no rollback path. Attendee rows are persisted even if eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees or email sending subsequently fails, leaving the booking's stored attendee list, the remote calendar event's attendee list, and the sent invitations permanently out of sync (added guests see the event in DB responses but were never invited or calendared).
B: The booking row is updated with createMany of attendees but the new attendee emails are never pushed to the existing calendar event attendees before eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees, and guests already present on the booking's calendar entry are not reconciled with the evt attendee list ordering. Depending on EventManager.updateCalendarAttendees semantics, the calendar event can be rebuilt with an attendee list that includes the just-created DB rows, so any failure between the Prisma update and the calendar update leaves the database and the external calendar event permanently out of sync (attendees on the booking but not invited on the calendar event), with no rollback of the created Attendee rows.

PAIR 4:
A: The write `prisma.booking.update({ where: { id: bookingId } })` re-derives authorization only from the earlier in-memory check with no ownership predicate in the update's where clause, and the guests are created before calendar/email work with no rollback path. Attendee rows are persisted even if eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees or email sending subsequently fails, leaving the booking's stored attendee list, the remote calendar event's attendee list, and the sent invitations permanently out of sync (added guests see the event in DB responses but were never invited or calendared).
B: Inconsistent error handling for side effects after the DB commit: `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` runs unguarded while the adjacent email call is wrapped in a swallow-everything catch; if the calendar update throws, the mutation rejects even though guests were persisted, and the user's retry hits the confusing `emails_must_be_unique_valid` BAD_REQUEST

PAIR 5:
A: The write `prisma.booking.update({ where: { id: bookingId } })` re-derives authorization only from the earlier in-memory check with no ownership predicate in the update's where clause, and the guests are created before calendar/email work with no rollback path. Attendee rows are persisted even if eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees or email sending subsequently fails, leaving the booking's stored attendee list, the remote calendar event's attendee list, and the sent invitations permanently out of sync (added guests see the event in DB responses but were never invited or calendared).
B: The handler's side effects aren't atomic: DB write → external calendar update (which can throw after persistence, leaving guests saved with an error returned to the client) → swallowed emails; separating an `addGuestsToBooking` service from the tRPC handler would make the sequencing and failure modes explicit.

PAIR 6:
A: The BAD_REQUEST message 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' is reused for the all-guests-filtered condition, where the emails are actually unique and valid — they were merely already attending or blacklisted. A user who submits an already-invited guest is told their email must be unique and valid, misdirecting them to retype a valid address instead of revealing the guest is already on the booking; after the unguarded calendar-failure path it also misreports an already-persisted add as an input-format error, sending debugging in the wrong direction.
B: The BAD_REQUEST thrown when uniqueGuests is empty reuses 'emails_must_be_unique_valid', but the actual condition is that every submitted guest was already an attendee or blacklisted — not that the emails are malformed or duplicated. A user who re-submits valid, unique addresses — for example retrying after the calendar-update failure in the non-atomic flow — is told their correctly-formatted emails are invalid, misdirecting debugging and hiding that the first attempt already added the guests.

PAIR 7:
A: The BAD_REQUEST message 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' is reused for the all-guests-filtered condition, where the emails are actually unique and valid — they were merely already attending or blacklisted. A user who submits an already-invited guest is told their email must be unique and valid, misdirecting them to retype a valid address instead of revealing the guest is already on the booking; after the unguarded calendar-failure path it also misreports an already-persisted add as an input-format error, sending debugging in the wrong direction.
B: When uniqueGuests.length === 0 after filtering, the handler throws TRPCError BAD_REQUEST "emails_must_be_unique_valid", but that condition also covers the case where every requested guest already exists as an attendee. A user who retries after a partially-failed earlier request (attendees persisted, calendar/emails failed — see the no-rollback finding) gets 'emails must be unique and valid' even though their input is perfectly valid and unique; the wrong-shape, wrong-content error misdirects debugging and blocks the retry that would be needed to complete the calendar update and emails.

PAIR 8:
A: The existing-attendee dedup compares guest === attendee.email case-sensitively while attendee emails are stored exactly as entered, so the write path and the compare path disagree on canonical form. Re-adding an existing attendee with different casing (John@X.com vs john@x.com) passes the filter, creating a duplicate Attendee row for the same person, who then receives both a full AttendeeScheduledEmail (as a 'new' guest) and an AttendeeAddGuestsEmail (as an existing one) for the same event.
B: Dedupe vs existing attendees uses exact match, so case/whitespace variants create duplicate attendees for the same person

PAIR 9:
A: The existing-attendee dedup compares guest === attendee.email case-sensitively while attendee emails are stored exactly as entered, so the write path and the compare path disagree on canonical form. Re-adding an existing attendee with different casing (John@X.com vs john@x.com) passes the filter, creating a duplicate Attendee row for the same person, who then receives both a full AttendeeScheduledEmail (as a 'new' guest) and an AttendeeAddGuestsEmail (as an existing one) for the same event.
B: P2 — Server schema is weaker than the client contract: `guests` array has no uniqueness validation or case normalization, so duplicate or case-variant emails produce duplicate attendee rows, duplicate emails, and duplicated ICS attendees

PAIR 10:
A: The isAttendee permission check compares attendee.email === user.email with exact case-sensitive string equality, though attendee emails are stored exactly as typed at booking time. A user whose account email casing differs from the mixed-case email they booked with (attendee rows are not normalized) is denied with FORBIDDEN even though they are a legitimate attendee of the booking, while the same email matched case-insensitively elsewhere in the codebase.
B: Attendee identity check uses exact non-normalized email match (attendee.email === user.email), so case differences can cause legitimate organizers/co-attendees to fail the isAttendee check

PAIR 11:
A: Server schema lacks the intra-request uniqueness validation the client enforces — duplicate emails like `["dup@x.com", "dup@x.com"]` pass both the server schema and the handler's `uniqueGuests` filter (which only dedups against existing attendees), hitting `createMany` and either violating the `(bookingId, email)` unique constraint (unhandled Prisma error → 500) or creating duplicate attendee rows and duplicate emails/invites
B: Server-side validation gap: input array is not deduped or case-normalized, so User@Example.com vs user@example.com creates duplicate attendee rows

PAIR 12:
A: Server schema lacks the intra-request uniqueness validation the client enforces — duplicate emails like `["dup@x.com", "dup@x.com"]` pass both the server schema and the handler's `uniqueGuests` filter (which only dedups against existing attendees), hitting `createMany` and either violating the `(bookingId, email)` unique constraint (unhandled Prisma error → 500) or creating duplicate attendee rows and duplicate emails/invites
B: Uniqueness/dedupe logic scattered across three layers — duplicates within the input guests array are not filtered server-side; server schema should be the single source of truth

PAIR 13:
A: sendAddGuestsEmails sends emails to all attendees (existing + new) plus organizer and team members on every invocation, awaited synchronously in the request path, causing response latency to grow linearly with attendee count and quadratic total email volume
B: Synchronous email sending in mutation path: await sendAddGuestsEmails serially renders N email payloads, multiplying latency with attendee count; should be backgrounded/queued
